one_line: Two-hour LLM inference workshop covering KV-cache memory math, prefill vs decode, attention variants, quantization, vLLM/SGLang serving optimizations, and benchmark caveats.
summary: A beginner-to-intermediate workshop that builds LLM inference costs from first principles. The speakers show that GPU memory splits into fixed model weights plus a KV-cache budget, and that KV-cache size per user sets the trade-off between context length and concurrency. They explain prefill (compute-bound, sets time to first token) versus decode (memory-bound, sets inter-token latency). They walk through model-side levers (weight quantization, GQA/MLA attention) and serving-side levers (paged KV blocks, continuous batching, prefix caching, KV quantization, speculative decoding). A benchmark on Mistral 7B and an agentic branching test compare vLLM and SGLang, with the speakers concluding that vLLM is the default and SGLang may win on agent loops. Several figures were corrected or are garbled in the captions, and the speakers say their own benchmark setup is workload-dependent.

key_ideas.idea: Inference cost is a recurring operating cost, and only two levers reduce it: use fewer tokens, or serve tokens more efficiently.
key_ideas.detail: The speakers frame inference as a per-user, per-token cost that scales with use, unlike one-time training. They say the two ways to cut it are to reduce token usage or to optimize the serving stack.

key_ideas.idea: Three pain points drive serving design: memory grows with context and users, time to first token grows with context, and throughput is capped by concurrency.
key_ideas.detail: The live demo on a 102 GB GPU shows KV memory rising with each added input. Naive serving handles requests one after another, which limits users per second.

key_ideas.idea: KV cache per user sets how many users fit on a GPU.
key_ideas.detail: After weights and overhead are subtracted, the leftover VRAM holds the key and value vectors. For Mistral 7B the speaker gives about 131 KB per token, roughly 0.5 GB per user at 4K context and about 2.1 GB at 16K. Concurrency is leftover memory divided by per-user KV size, so context length and user count trade off directly.

key_ideas.idea: Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, which explains TTFT and inter-token latency.
key_ideas.detail: Prefill builds KV for the whole prompt in one heavy pass, so its time is the TTFT and rises with prompt length. Decode computes attention for one new token per step but reads the whole KV history each time, so its arithmetic intensity is low and it is limited by memory bandwidth.

key_ideas.idea: Serving targets force a trade-off between quality, latency and throughput; fix the binding constraint first.
key_ideas.detail: For premium chat, fix the latency SLO and then count how many concurrent users fit. For async agent work, fix the minimum batch and accept higher latency. The speakers say an expensive GPU can still give the lowest cost per million tokens once batch throughput is counted.

key_ideas.idea: Attention design changes KV size: moving from MHA to GQA to MLA shrinks the cache at some quality cost.
key_ideas.detail: Multi-query attention keeps one KV head and loses quality. Grouped-query attention, such as 32 query heads sharing 8 KV heads, gives about 4x less KV with near-MHA quality. Multi-head latent attention compresses K and V into a latent vector; the speaker first said 56x but corrected it to about 14x versus MHA.

key_ideas.idea: Paged KV blocks and continuous batching are the main serving wins, and vLLM ships both by default.
key_ideas.detail: Paging maps logical KV positions to physical blocks allocated on demand, which avoids contiguous-allocation waste. Continuous batching admits new requests as earlier ones finish so the GPU does not sit idle. Prefix caching and KV quantization stack on top.

key_ideas.idea: Exact-hash prefix caching misses on small prompt edits; a radix tree reuses the longest shared prefix and suits agent loops.
key_ideas.detail: Hash-based prefix caches need an exact match, so changing one word causes a miss. A radix tree stores shared prefixes as a tree and matches partial overlaps. This matters in agent loops that resend the same long system prompt many times. The speakers say SGLang uses this approach.

key_ideas.idea: On plain chat traffic vLLM and SGLang tie, but on repeated agentic branching SGLang was 3-4x faster in the speakers' test.
key_ideas.detail: On ShareGPT prompts they saw no statistical difference. In a multi-round loop that generates a proposal and then reviews and scores it, SGLang pulled ahead. The speakers say setup can change the result and advise vLLM as the default for standard APIs.

techniques.name: KV-cache capacity planning
techniques.how: Subtract weights and overhead from VRAM to get the KV budget. Compute KV bytes per token as 2 x head_dim x layers x KV_heads x bytes_per_value. Max concurrent users = budget / (KV bytes per token x context length). Use the result to choose context limit and batch size before picking hardware.
techniques.when: Sizing a self-hosted deployment or deciding how many users one GPU can carry at a given context length.

techniques.name: Fix one dimension, then solve the rest for cost
techniques.how: Pick the binding constraint first: a latency SLO for interactive chat, or a minimum batch size for async agents. Then solve for the other dimensions, compute cost per million tokens for each candidate GPU, and compare.
techniques.when: Choosing GPU hardware or a serving config for a known workload shape.

techniques.name: Weight quantization for KV headroom
techniques.how: Move weights from FP16 to INT8, INT4 or NF4 to shrink the model footprint, which leaves more VRAM for KV cache. Validate quality with an external benchmark, since quantization does not come free.
techniques.when: The model does not fit, or you need more concurrency or context on the same GPU.

techniques.name: Attention variant selection
techniques.how: Prefer GQA over MHA for a roughly 4x KV reduction with little quality loss. Consider MLA for larger savings. Treat MQA as a last resort because quality drops.
techniques.when: Designing or choosing a model for memory-bound, long-context serving.

techniques.name: Radix-tree prefix caching for agent loops
techniques.how: Store the KV of shared prompt prefixes in a radix tree so partial prefix matches reuse cache. Keep system prompts and tool definitions stable across calls so the prefix stays shared.
techniques.when: Many calls share long prompts, such as agent loops that resend the same instructions.

techniques.name: Speculative decoding variants
techniques.how: A small draft model proposes several tokens and the target model accepts or rejects them. EAGLE trains a small head on the target's hidden features. Medusa uses parallel heads to draft several tokens at once. Test on your own workload, because the speakers doubt the gain for plain draft-model decoding.
techniques.when: Decode latency matters and outputs are predictable, such as code. Verify the gain before adopting it.

techniques.name: Engine benchmarking loop
techniques.how: For each config, restart the server, load the model, send a fixed prompt set, and scrape engine metrics for KV usage, TTFT, inter-token latency and throughput. Include a multi-round agentic test, not only single-shot prompts. The speakers say one full run takes about an hour.
techniques.when: Comparing serving engines or settings before a production choice.

numbers.claim: Inference market cited at about $23B today.
GPT-3 training cited at about $4.6M as a one-time cost; the speaker says inference is the recurring cost that scales with use. The stat is attributed to OpenAI as old but still true.

Speaker cites a Semianalysis estimate of about $36B for running Google-scale search on LLMs, with a per-query target under 0.5 cents. The captions are garbled here, so treat the figures as unverified.
Mistral 7B KV cache about 131 KB per token: 32 layers, 128-dim vectors, 8 KV heads at 16-bit.
KV cache about 0.5 GB per user at 4K context and about 2.1 GB at 16K. About 80 users at 4K fit in roughly 42 GB of KV cache.
GPT-OSS-120B BF16 weights about 240 GB, which the speaker says compress to about 65 GB in MXFP4 so they fit on one 80 GB H100.
Quantizing Mistral 7B to INT4 reduces weight memory to about 4.5 GB, from about 15 GB at FP16. The speaker reports these as theoretical numbers with no throughput test.
GQA with 8 KV heads instead of 32 gives about 4x KV compression.
MLA is about 14x KV savings versus MHA. The speaker first said 56x and corrected it on the spot after finding a missed layer multiplier.
HF Transformers baseline on H100: about 51 tokens/s throughput, TTFT 54, inter-token latency 19 (units as spoken).
vLLM with default paging, continuous batching and KV caching gives about 15x the baseline throughput.
SGLang versus vLLM on an agentic branching test (generate, then review and score, repeated): about 3-4x better for SGLang in the speakers' setup. No statistical difference on ShareGPT prompts.

hot_takes: The speaker says speculative decoding did not help in his own tests, mainly because the draft model and target model have alignment problems.
vLLM is the production default for standard API traffic, but SGLang may be the better choice for agentic workloads with repeated prompts.
Expensive GPUs can still be the cheapest per million tokens once batch throughput is counted.
Most KV-cache optimization research is a fast-moving area, and the speaker expects a separate KV-cache engineering discipline to form.

relevance.why: InferCraft (L2B) is a vLLM plus Ray Serve stack with KV strategies, EAGLE-3 and quantization on one RTX 5090. The talk gives the capacity formula, the engine comparison and the agentic-workload caveat that bear on which engine and KV settings InferCraft should default to.
relevance.action: Add a KV capacity calculator for the RTX 5090 (32 GB) using the talk's formula, then benchmark vLLM against SGLang on a multi-round agent-branching workload with prefix hit rate and TTFT logged, before InferCraft fixes its default engine.

relevance.why: ProsHarness re-sends long planning and critique prefixes across loops. The talk's point that exact-hash prefix caches miss on small edits suggests keeping those prefixes byte-stable.
relevance.action: Keep the shared plan and critique prefix identical across ProsHarness loop iterations so any provider or local prefix cache can hit; avoid editing the header on every turn.

relevance.why: Recurring interest in evals and cheap-model pipelines. The talk's benchmark lesson is that single-shot prompts hid engine differences that appeared only in a multi-round workload.
relevance.action: When benchmarking a cheap-model pipeline, include a multi-round, agent-style test case, not just single-shot prompts.
